question.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ){|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =4([0-1]-[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]) \\  & =4(\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$
